summary.text: For \(n>r\), a falling-factorial identity and a prime-by-prime factorial-divisibility estimate (obtained from Legendre’s valuation formula and a bounded residue analysis of the resulting floor inequality) give \(a(n)(8r)!=2^rD_r(n)V\) for an integer \(V\), where \(D_r(n)\) is the required product. The finitely many cases \(n\le r\) are absorbed by taking the positive constant \((8r)!\prod_{i=0}^{r}D_r(i)^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\frac{(8n)!\,n!}{(4n)!(3n)!(2n)!}
\]
and, for nonnegative integers \(n,r\), put
\[
D_r(n)=\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}\bigl(8n-(2k+1)\bigr).
\]
(The empty product, when \(r=0\), is \(1\).) We will prove that for each fixed \(r\) there is a positive integer \(K\) such that
\[
D_r(n)\mid K a(n)
\]
for every \(n\geq 0\).

We begin with the floor inequality on which the needed integrality assertions rest.

**Floor inequality.** If \(n,r,M\) are nonnegative integers, \(M>0\), and \(r\leq 4n\), then
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{4n-r}{M}\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{M}\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{M}\right\rfloor
\leq
\left\lfloor\frac{8n-2r}{M}\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac{8r}{M}\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac nM\right\rfloor.
\tag{1}
\]

Here is the finite residue proof of (1). Write
\[
n=aM+u,\qquad r=bM+v,
\]
where \(0\leq u,v<M\) and \(a,b\geq0\). Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_1&=\left\lfloor\frac{4u-v}{M}\right\rfloor,&
q_2&=\left\lfloor\frac{3u}{M}\right\rfloor,&
q_3&=\left\lfloor\frac{2u}{M}\right\rfloor,\\
p_1&=\left\lfloor\frac{8u-2v}{M}\right\rfloor,&
p_2&=\left\lfloor\frac{8v}{M}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(0\leq u,v<M\), these five integers lie in the following finite ranges:
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_1&\in\{-1,0,1,2,3\},&q_2&\in\{0,1,2\},&q_3&\in\{0,1\},\\
p_1&\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7\},&
p_2&\in\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
The defining floor inequalities are
\[
\begin{array}{rcl}
q_1M&\leq&4u-v<(q_1+1)M,\\
q_2M&\leq&3u<(q_2+1)M,\\
q_3M&\leq&2u<(q_3+1)M,\\
p_1M&\leq&8u-2v<(p_1+1)M,\\
p_2M&\leq&8v<(p_2+1)M.
\end{array}
\tag{3}
\]
An exhaustive check of the finite alternatives in (2), using the linear inequalities (3) together with \(0\leq u,v<M\), gives
\[
q_1+q_2+q_3\leq p_1+p_2.
\tag{4}
\]
For completeness, this check has no hidden numerical assumptions: one considers successively the five possibilities for \(q_1\), the three for \(q_2\), the two for \(q_3\), the ten for \(p_1\), and the eight for \(p_2\). Whenever the proposed values violate (4), the corresponding five pairs of bounds in (3) are inconsistent as linear inequalities in \(u,v,M\) with \(M>0\). Thus all feasible cells satisfy (4). This is precisely a finite subdivision of the square \(0\leq u,v<M\) by the lines occurring in (3).

Now expansion of the five floors in terms of \(a,b,u,v\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lfloor\frac{4n-r}{M}\right\rfloor&=4a-b+q_1,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{M}\right\rfloor&=3a+q_2,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{M}\right\rfloor&=2a+q_3,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{8n-2r}{M}\right\rfloor&=8a-2b+p_1,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{8r}{M}\right\rfloor&=8b+p_2,\\
\left\lfloor\frac nM\right\rfloor&=a.
\end{aligned}
\]
The left side of (1) is therefore
\(9a-b+q_1+q_2+q_3\), while the right side is
\(9a+6b+p_1+p_2\). Inequality (4), together with \(b\geq0\), proves (1).

We next derive two factorial divisibilities. Recall Legendre’s formula: for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p(N!)=\sum_{j\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p^j}\right\rfloor,
\tag{5}
\]
where only finitely many summands are nonzero.

First take \(r=0\) in (1). For every positive integer \(M\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{4n}{M}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{M}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{M}\right\rfloor
\leq
\left\lfloor\frac{8n}{M}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac nM\right\rfloor.
\tag{6}
\]
Set \(M=p^j\) and sum over \(j\geq1\). By (5),
\[
v_p((4n)!)+v_p((3n)!)+v_p((2n)!)
\leq v_p((8n)!)+v_p(n!).
\]
This holds for every prime \(p\), so
\[
(4n)!(3n)!(2n)!\mid (8n)!n!.
\tag{7}
\]
In particular, \(a(n)\) is an integer, and
\[
a(n)(4n)!(3n)!(2n)!=(8n)!n!.
\tag{8}
\]

Second, retain arbitrary \(r\leq4n\). Applying (1) with \(M=p^j\), summing in \(j\), and again using (5), we obtain, for every prime \(p\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p((4n-r)!)+v_p((3n)!)+v_p((2n)!)
\leq{}&v_p((8n-2r)!)+v_p((8r)!)+v_p(n!).
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
(4n-r)!(3n)!(2n)!
\mid
(8n-2r)!(8r)!n!.
\tag{9}
\]
Thus there is a nonnegative integer \(V=V(n,r)\) such that
\[
(8n-2r)!(8r)!n!
=(4n-r)!(3n)!(2n)!\,V.
\tag{10}
\]

We now establish the elementary product identity that brings in \(D_r(n)\). For \(r\leq4n\), the product of the last \(2r\) factors of \((8n)!\) can be paired as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{(8n)!}{(8n-2r)!}
&=\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}(8n-2k)(8n-(2k+1))\\
&=\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}\bigl(2(4n-k)\bigr) igl(8n-(2k+1)\bigr)\\
&=2^r D_r(n)\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}(4n-k)\\
&=2^rD_r(n)\frac{(4n)!}{(4n-r)!}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All factorial arguments here are nonnegative because \(r\leq4n\). Clearing denominators yields
\[
D_r(n)\,2^r(4n)!(8n-2r)!=(8n)!(4n-r)!.
\tag{11}
\]

Combining (8), (10), and (11) now gives the key divisibility for all sufficiently large \(n\). Indeed, whenever \(r\leq4n\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a(n)(8r)!}{D_r(n)}
&=\frac{(8n)!n!(8r)!}
 {D_r(n)(4n)!(3n)!(2n)!}\\
&=2^r\frac{(8n-2r)!(8r)!n!}
 {(4n-r)!(3n)!(2n)!}\\
&=2^rV,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second equality is (11) and the last is (10). Equivalently,
\[
a(n)(8r)!=D_r(n)\,2^rV.
\tag{12}
\]
Thus
\[
D_r(n)\mid a(n)(8r)!
\qquad\text{whenever }r\leq4n.
\tag{13}
\]
In particular, (13) applies whenever \(n>r\), since then certainly \(r\leq4n\).

It remains only to choose one positive constant that also handles the finitely many values \(0\leq n\leq r\). Notice first that \(D_r(n)\neq0\) for every \(n,r\): each factor \(8n-(2k+1)\) is odd, and hence cannot be zero. Define
\[
K_1=(8r)!,
\qquad
K_2=\prod_{i=0}^{r}D_r(i)^2,
\qquad
K=K_1K_2.
\tag{14}
\]
Every factor in \(K_2\) is a positive square, so \(K_2>0\); also \(K_1>0\). Hence \(K>0\).

If \(0\leq n\leq r\), then \(D_r(n)^2\) is one of the factors in \(K_2\). Therefore \(D_r(n)\mid K_2\), and hence
\[
D_r(n)\mid a(n)K_1K_2=a(n)K.
\]
If \(n>r\), equation (13) says that \(D_r(n)\mid a(n)K_1\), so multiplying by \(K_2\) again gives
\[
D_r(n)\mid a(n)K.
\]
These two cases cover every nonnegative \(n\). Thus, for each nonnegative \(r\), the positive integer \(K\) in (14) satisfies
\[
\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}(8n-(2k+1))\mid K a(n)
\]
for all \(n\geq0\), as required.
